title: What Happens When a CD Matures? Grace Period + Your 4 Options
meta_description: What happens when a CD matures? See how auto-renewal and the grace period work, plus your 4 options before your money is locked in again.
quick_answer: When a CD matures, its fixed term ends. Your principal and earned interest become available without an early withdrawal penalty, usually only during a short grace period set by the bank. During that window you can renew, switch terms, move the money or withdraw it. If you do nothing, many CDs automatically renew for a similar term at the bank's current rate, which may be lower.
key_takeaways: Look up your maturity date and the exact last day of your grace period today. Both are in your account disclosure and maturity notice, and grace periods differ from bank to bank.
If you do nothing, many CDs automatically renew at the bank's current rate for that term. That rate may be lower than what you were earning.
During the grace period you can usually renew, switch terms, move the money to a high-yield savings account or withdraw it, all without a penalty.
If you miss the window, the money is usually locked into a new term. Taking it out early can then cost an early withdrawal penalty, which at some banks can eat into your principal.
Every time you open or renew a CD, set three reminders: 30 days before maturity, on the maturity date, and a few days before the grace period ends.
who_this_is_for: This guide is for savers whose certificate of deposit (CD) matures soon, or who just got a maturity notice, and who want to know what happens by default and how to pick their next step before the grace period ends.
intro:
When your CD matures, your savings are free of early withdrawal penalties, but only for a short window. That moment is easy to miss. The maturity notice gets buried in your inbox, the grace period ends without any fuss, and the bank rolls your money into a new term at whatever rate it's offering that day.

This guide covers what happens by default when a CD matures, how the grace period works, and the four options you have. It also explains what to do if you've already missed the window and how to set up reminders so it doesn't happen again. It's general education based on US-style certificates of deposit. Terms differ by bank and by country, so always check the details in your own account documents.

steps.name: Find your maturity date and grace period end date
steps.text: Check your maturity notice, your original account disclosure, or the CD's account details page in online banking. Write down the exact last day of the grace period, and note whether the bank counts calendar days or business days.

steps.name: Confirm what happens by default
steps.text: Find out what happens if you do nothing. The CD may renew automatically (check which term it renews into) or pay out to a linked account. If it was a promotional CD, check whether it renews into a standard term at a standard rate.

steps.name: Check the renewal rate
steps.text: Look up the APY the bank will pay on the renewed CD. If the maturity notice doesn't show it yet, ask the bank when the rate will be set. It is usually the rate in effect on the maturity date.

steps.name: Compare your options side by side
steps.text: Compare the renewal rate with other CD terms at the same bank, CDs at other insured banks or credit unions, and high-yield savings accounts. For each option, note the APY, term length, early withdrawal penalty, minimum deposit and deposit insurance coverage.

steps.name: Match the choice to when you need the money
steps.text: Work out when you'll actually need the money. Money for a near-term goal or an emergency fund usually needs to stay easy to reach. Money you won't touch for years can be locked up for longer.

steps.name: Give the bank your instructions before the grace period ends
steps.text: Send your choice online, by phone or at a branch, ideally several days before the deadline, and ask whether there's a cut-off time on the last day. A short message works: 'Please do not renew my CD ending 1234 at maturity. Transfer the full balance to my checking account ending 5678 and confirm in writing.' Save the confirmation.

steps.name: Start transfers early if you're moving the money
steps.text: If the money is going to another bank, open the new account first and start the transfer early in the grace period. Transfers between banks can take a few business days, and the withdrawal from the CD needs to be processed before the window closes.

steps.name: Set reminders for the next maturity date
steps.text: As soon as the new CD or account is set up, add the next maturity date and grace period end date to your calendar. Set reminders for 30 days before, the maturity date itself, and a few days before the grace period ends.

sections.heading: What happens when a CD matures by default
paragraphs: By default, many CDs renew automatically when they mature. The bank moves your principal and interest into a new CD, usually for the same or a similar term, at whatever rate it pays for that term on the maturity date.

Maturity just means the CD's term has ended. On the maturity date your locked-in rate stops. Your balance (the original deposit plus any interest credited to the CD) can then be withdrawn without an early withdrawal penalty, but only during a limited window called the grace period.

The catch is the renewal rate. A renewed CD earns the bank's current rate, which may be lower than what you were earning and lower than what other banks or account types pay. Promotional and special-term CDs often catch people out, because some banks renew them into a standard term at a standard rate. The renewal section of your account disclosure tells you which rule applies to your CD.

Not every CD renews automatically. Some banks pay the balance into a linked savings or checking account at maturity, and some ask you to choose ahead of time. Brokered CDs, which you buy through an investment account, usually don't renew at all. The principal and final interest are typically paid into your brokerage account as cash.
bullets: Maturity date: the day the term ends and the fixed rate stops.
Automatic renewal: a new term starts at the bank's current rate unless you tell the bank otherwise.
Payout at maturity: some CDs pay into a linked account instead of renewing.
Brokered CDs: usually pay out to your brokerage account. Check your broker's rules.

sections.heading: How the CD grace period works (and why its length varies)
paragraphs: A CD grace period is a short window after maturity, set by each bank, when you can withdraw money from your CD, add to it or change it without an early withdrawal penalty.

There's no standard length. Many banks offer roughly one to two weeks, but some give less and some give more. The length can even differ between products at the same bank, and some banks count calendar days while others count business days. The only reliable sources are your account disclosure (the terms you received when you opened the CD) and the maturity notice the bank sends before the CD matures.

In the US, federal Truth in Savings rules generally require banks to send advance notice before an automatically renewing CD matures, for most terms longer than one month. If you've switched to paperless documents, that notice may only show up in your online banking secure inbox, so check there as well as your email. Outside the US, fixed-term deposits (often called term deposits or fixed-rate bonds) follow local rules, so check your bank's terms and your national regulator.

What you're allowed to do during the grace period also varies. Most banks allow a full withdrawal, and many also allow partial withdrawals, extra deposits or a change of term. Interest during the window differs too. Some banks pay the new rate from the maturity date, while others pay a different rate, or nothing, on money you withdraw. If that matters to you, ask your bank.
bullets: Account disclosure: search for 'renewal', 'maturity' or 'grace period'.
Maturity notice: arrives before maturity and shows the renewal terms, often including the grace period.
Online banking: the CD's account details page often shows the maturity date.
Customer service: ask, 'What is the exact last day of my grace period, and is there a cut-off time?'

sections.heading: Your 4 options during the grace period
paragraphs: During the grace period you have four main options: renew the CD, switch to a different term, move the money to a high-yield savings account, or withdraw it. If your bank allows partial withdrawals, you can also combine them, for example by withdrawing part and renewing the rest.

Option 1: Renew for the same term. Renewing keeps the money in a fixed-rate CD of the same length at the same bank. It takes the least effort, but the new rate may be lower than your old one, and the money is locked up again until the next maturity date. If you renew, check the new rate first so that renewing is something you chose, not something that happened by default.

Option 2: Switch terms. Switching moves the balance into a CD with a different length or different features, either at your current bank or at another insured bank or credit union. A shorter term gets the money back to you sooner. A longer term fixes your rate for longer but also ties up your money for longer. Some banks offer no-penalty CDs, which allow early withdrawals under set conditions, or bump-up CDs, which may let you request a higher rate. These variations may start at a lower rate or come with conditions, so compare the details.

Option 3: Move the money to a high-yield savings account. This gives up a fixed rate in exchange for flexibility. You can usually add or withdraw money at any time, but the rate is variable and the bank can change it whenever it likes. Make sure the account is at an FDIC-insured bank or NCUA-insured credit union, and check for minimum balances, fees and transfer limits.

Option 4: Withdraw the money. Withdrawing pays your principal and interest into a checking or savings account. It makes sense when the money was set aside for a planned expense, such as a home down payment, tuition or a car, or when you've decided to use it for something else. Cash left in a regular checking account may earn little or nothing, so if you don't need it right away, consider moving it to an account that earns interest.
bullets: Renew: least effort, but the rate may drop and the money is locked up again.
Switch terms: match the term to your timeline and compare penalties.
High-yield savings: easy access, but the rate can change.
Withdraw: full access for a planned use, but idle cash may earn little.

sections.heading: How to decide which option fits you
paragraphs: The right option usually comes down to three things: when you'll need the money, how the renewal rate compares with your alternatives, and how much flexibility you want.

Start with your timeline. Money you might need within months, such as an emergency fund, usually belongs somewhere easy to reach. Money you won't touch for years can be locked up for longer. Then compare the actual numbers: the annual percentage yield (APY) on the renewal against other terms, other banks and savings accounts, plus each product's early withdrawal penalty and minimum deposit.

Be careful about trying to time interest rates, because no one can reliably predict them. A longer fixed term protects you if rates fall, but you're stuck with it if they rise. A flexible account works the other way around. Many savers deal with this uncertainty by spreading money across several terms instead of betting on one outcome.

This is general information, not personal financial advice. For large balances, retirement accounts or tax questions, consider talking to a licensed financial adviser or tax professional in your country.
bullets: When will I need this money?
What APY will the renewal pay, and how does it compare with other terms, banks and savings accounts?
What's the early withdrawal penalty on the new product?
Right now, do I care more about a fixed rate or about easy access?
Will this keep me within the deposit insurance limit at this bank or credit union?

sections.heading: What happens if you miss the grace period
paragraphs: If you miss the grace period, an automatically renewing CD is usually locked into a new term. Taking the money out before that term ends usually means paying an early withdrawal penalty.

Each bank sets its own early withdrawal penalty. It's usually a set amount of interest, such as a certain number of days' or months' worth, and it's often bigger for longer terms. At some banks, if you haven't yet earned enough interest to cover the penalty, the rest comes out of your principal. That means breaking a CD that just renewed can give you back less than you put in.

If you've only just missed the deadline, call the bank first. Ask whether it can still change the term or release the money without a penalty. Some banks are flexible if you're only slightly late, but that's up to them, so don't count on it.

If the bank can't help, do the math before you act. Ask for the exact penalty in dollars, then estimate how much extra interest you'd earn elsewhere over the rest of the new term. Here's a hypothetical example with made-up numbers. Say a $10,000 CD just renewed at 3% APY, and the penalty is 90 days of interest. The penalty is roughly $74. Moving the money to an account that pays 1 percentage point more for the remaining 11 months would earn roughly $92 extra before tax. That's a net gain of under $20, and even less if a variable rate drops. If you need the money for an emergency, the penalty may simply be the price of getting it.
bullets: What's my exact penalty in dollars if I withdraw today?
Can the penalty come out of my principal?
Can I make a partial withdrawal, and how is the penalty calculated on it?
Do any of the penalty waivers listed in my disclosure apply to me?

sections.heading: How to set up reminders so you never miss a maturity date
paragraphs: The simplest way to never miss a CD maturity date is to set three reminders the day you open or renew a CD: 30 days before maturity, on the maturity date, and a few days before the grace period ends.

Each reminder has its own job. The 30-day reminder gives you time to compare rates and open a new account if you plan to move the money. The maturity-day reminder prompts you to check that the CD has matured and your instructions are in place. The last reminder, a few days before the grace period ends, is your final chance to act while a transfer can still go through.
Put the grace period end date in your calendar, not just the maturity date. That date decides whether you make a penalty-free choice or get locked into a renewal.
bullets: Give each calendar event a clear name, for example 'CD at [Bank], account ending 1234: grace period ends, act by noon'.
Turn on account alerts in online banking, and check whether maturity notices come by mail, by email or to a secure inbox.
If your bank allows it, set your maturity instructions online in advance so the default never kicks in by accident.

Keep a simple tracker in a spreadsheet, notes app or Notion database with columns for bank, balance, term, APY, open date, maturity date, grace period end date, default action and the action you chose. Don't store full account numbers or logins in it.
Share the tracker or calendar with a spouse, partner or other trusted person so someone else knows the dates.

sections.heading: Reinvesting? Consider a CD ladder
paragraphs: If you plan to reinvest when a CD matures, a CD ladder makes each maturity date a routine decision instead of a scramble.

A CD ladder spreads your savings across several CDs that mature at different times, so part of the money becomes available at regular intervals. For example, someone might split a balance across one-, two- and three-year CDs. As each CD (each 'rung' of the ladder) matures, they decide whether to extend it, move it or use the cash.

A ladder gives you regular access to part of your savings and means you don't lock everything in at one rate. It also means more accounts and more maturity dates to keep track of, which is why the reminder system above matters. Our [CD ladder guide](/cd-ladder-guide) shows how to build and maintain one, step by step.
bullets: Pros: regular access to part of your money, and you're not relying on a single rate.
Cons: more accounts to track, and breaking any rung early still costs a penalty.

sections.heading: Taxes, deposit insurance and IRA CDs: what else to check
paragraphs: Before you act on a maturing CD, check three things that can change the outcome: tax on the interest, deposit insurance limits and, if the CD is in an IRA, the rules for retirement accounts.

In the US, CD interest is generally taxed as ordinary income in the year it's credited or made available to you, whether or not you withdraw it. Banks usually report it on Form 1099-INT. Tax treatment differs by country and account type, so check with your tax authority or a tax professional.

In the US, deposits at FDIC-insured banks and NCUA-insured credit unions are protected up to the standard limit. At the time of writing, that's $250,000 per depositor, per insured institution, per ownership category. Confirm the current limit at FDIC.gov or NCUA.gov. If renewing or combining accounts would push your balance at one institution over the limit, check your coverage with the FDIC's or NCUA's online tools. Other countries have their own deposit guarantee schemes with different limits and rules.

If your CD is held inside an IRA, maturity doesn't change its status as a retirement account, but how you move the money does matter. Money is usually moved to another institution by a direct transfer between custodians. Withdrawing it yourself can trigger taxes or penalties, depending on your age and the rules, so ask your custodian before you do anything.
bullets: Interest: in the US, generally taxable when it's credited, even if you leave it in the CD.
Insurance: confirm your coverage before combining balances at one institution.
IRA CDs: ask about a direct transfer between custodians before moving the money.

recommendations.best_for: Savers with several CDs or a CD ladder who want one tracker for maturity dates, grace period end dates, APYs, default actions and chosen actions. Date fields in a Notion database can be set to send reminders, so the tracker can double as your alert system. Confirm current features and pricing on Notion's website.
recommendations.not_for: Anyone with just one CD, since a phone calendar reminder is simpler. It also won't suit anyone who wants rates tracked automatically. Notion doesn't connect to your bank or watch rates for you, and you shouldn't store full account numbers or login details in it.

faq.question: How long is the grace period when a CD matures?
faq.answer: There's no set length. Each bank chooses its own, and it can differ between products. Many banks offer roughly one to two weeks, but check the exact end date in your account disclosure or maturity notice, and find out whether the bank counts calendar days or business days.

faq.question: Will my CD automatically renew at the same rate?
faq.answer: Usually not. An automatically renewing CD typically moves into a new term at the bank's current rate for that term on the maturity date, which could be higher or lower than your original rate. Promotional CDs may renew into a standard product at a standard rate, so check your maturity notice.

faq.question: Can I add money to my CD when it matures?
faq.answer: Many banks let you add money during the grace period, but not all of them do, and some limit how much you can add. Check your disclosure or ask the bank before the grace period ends. Outside the grace period, most traditional CDs don't accept extra deposits.

faq.question: Is CD interest taxed when the CD matures?
faq.answer: In the US, CD interest is generally taxable in the year it's credited or made available to you, not only when the CD matures. Banks usually report it on Form 1099-INT, so you may owe tax on interest from a multi-year CD before you withdraw it. Rules differ by country and account type (CDs held inside IRAs, for example), so check with a tax professional.

faq.question: What happens to a brokered CD when it matures?
faq.answer: Brokered CDs usually don't renew automatically. At maturity, the principal and final interest are typically paid into your brokerage account as cash, and from there you can reinvest or withdraw it. Before maturity, you generally can't cash a brokered CD in early the way you can with a bank CD. You may be able to sell it on the secondary market, possibly for less than you paid, so check your broker's rules.

faq.question: Can I get out of a CD that renewed automatically?
faq.answer: Once the grace period is over, you usually can't without paying the early withdrawal penalty on the new term. If you've only just missed the deadline, call the bank and ask whether it will make an exception, but don't count on it. Ask for the exact penalty in dollars and compare it with the extra interest you'd realistically earn by moving the money.

conclusion: When your CD matures, you have a decision to make, and doing nothing counts as a decision. Find the maturity date and the last day of the grace period, check what your bank does by default, and compare the renewal rate with your other options. Then give the bank your instructions before the window closes and set reminders for the next maturity date. If you're reinvesting across several CDs, our [CD ladder guide](/cd-ladder-guide) shows how to stagger maturity dates so each one becomes a simple, routine choice. Account terms, rates and tax rules change and differ by bank and country, so confirm the details with your bank. For personal decisions about large balances, retirement accounts or taxes, a licensed adviser or tax professional can help.
